\chapter{Mirar Y Moverse}
\label{ch:es-mover}
\hlchaptermodality{446}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can arrange to go somewhere with somebody and talk about what we watched, keeping ver apart from mirar and mover apart from trasladar.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[mirar]{mirar — pointing the eyes on purpose}

\label{lesson:ES-C446-mirar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{mira}, the little word that opens a sentence. Say \textbf{ver} and \textbf{el ojo}. \emph{Mira} is an order from a verb you have never been given. Name it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: mirar}
\textbf{mirar} — to look, to look at, to watch.

\emph{Mírame} — look at me. \emph{Estaba mirando por la ventana} — I was looking out of the window. \emph{Mirar la tele} is to watch television, though \emph{ver la tele} is commoner in Spain.

\textbf{mira} and \textbf{mire} — the forms you already use to mean \emph{look…}, \emph{listen…} — are this verb told to somebody, nothing more. You have been giving an order for chapters without knowing which verb it came from.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: ver and mirar are not interchangeable}]
English has this split too and hides it, because \emph{see} and \emph{look at} feel like one idea. They are not.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{what it describes} \\
\midrule
\textbf{ver} & the eyes \textbf{receive} — it happens to you \\
\textbf{mirar} & the eyes are \textbf{aimed} — you do it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Veo el mar desde aquí} — I can see the sea from here, whether or not I meant to. \emph{Miro el mar} — I am looking at it, deliberately.

So \emph{ver} belongs with \emph{oír} (to hear) and \emph{mirar} with \emph{escuchar} (to listen). The test is whether you chose: if you could have not done it, the verb is \emph{mirar}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{mīrārī} meant \textbf{to wonder at, to be amazed} — not to look at all. The looking came from the wondering: you stare at what astonishes you, and after enough centuries the staring is all that is left.

The wonder survives in the relatives:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the wonder in it} \\
\midrule
\textbf{el milagro} & a miracle — a thing wondered at \\
\textbf{admirar} & to admire — to wonder \textbf{at} \\
mirar & to look \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English took the same root for \textbf{miracle}, \textbf{admire}, \textbf{marvel} and \textbf{mirage} — a thing that astonishes you and is not there.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mirar}
  \item I can see the sea from here, and I am looking at it
  \item what \emph{mīrārī} meant before it meant looking
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To look at? (\textbf{Mirar}.) Which verb is it, when you say \emph{mira}? (\textbf{This one, as an order}.) What did the Latin mean? (\textbf{To wonder at}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mover]{mover — and the phone that is named after it}

\label{lesson:ES-C446-mover}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el móvil} and \textbf{trasladar}. Say \textbf{mirar}. Your phone is called \emph{móvil} for a reason. Name the verb inside it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: mover}
\textbf{mover} — to move something. \textbf{moverse} — to move yourself.

\emph{¿Me ayudas a mover la mesa?} — will you help me move the table? \emph{No te muevas} — do not move. \emph{El niño no para de moverse} — the child will not sit still.

The stem breaks under stress, like \emph{doler} and \emph{dormir}: \textbf{muevo}, \textbf{mueves}, \textbf{mueve}, but \emph{movemos}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{movēre}, to move. \textbf{El móvil} is \emph{mōbilis} — \textbf{movable} — from the same verb, so a mobile phone is literally \emph{the movable one}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the movement in it} \\
\midrule
mover & to move it \\
\textbf{el móvil} & the movable thing \\
el automóvil & the \textbf{self}-moving thing \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That last one is the whole of \emph{automobile} explained: \emph{auto-} from Greek \emph{autós}, self, on a Latin stem. A car is a thing that moves without being pulled.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Mover} and \textbf{trasladar} are not the same act, and a notice picks carefully.

\emph{Mover} is physical and local: shift the table, shift your arm. \emph{Trasladar} is institutional and from-somewhere-to-somewhere: the office was moved, the patient was transferred. You \emph{mueves} a chair across a room; a company \emph{traslada} its headquarters.

Use \emph{mover} for a thing you could push with your hands, and \emph{trasladar} when an address changes. Getting it backwards is not a grammar mistake — it is a register mistake, and it is the kind a reader notices.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mover}, then \emph{muevo}
  \item will you help me move the table
  \item why a phone is called \emph{el móvil}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To move something? (\textbf{Mover}.) The \emph{yo} form? (\textbf{Muevo}.) What does \emph{móvil} mean literally? (\textbf{Movable}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[acompañar]{acompañar — going as the one who shares bread}

\label{lesson:ES-C446-acompanar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{el compañero} and recall what it is made of. Say \textbf{mover}. Turn the companion into something you do.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: acompañar}
\textbf{acompañar} — to go with somebody, to accompany.

\emph{Te acompaño} — I will come with you, and also \emph{I am here with you} at a funeral. \emph{¿Me acompañas al médico?} — will you come with me to the doctor? \emph{Acompañado de} — accompanied by, on a form or a menu.

It is the ordinary way to offer to come along, and it is warmer than the English \emph{accompany}, which sounds formal.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{a-} plus \textbf{compañ-} plus \textbf{-ar}, and the middle is the word you already took apart.

\textbf{el compañero} is \emph{com-} together plus \emph{pānis}, bread — \textbf{the one you share bread with}. So \emph{acompañar} is \textbf{to go along as that person}, and a Spanish speaker offering \emph{te acompaño} is, at root, offering to share a meal's worth of company.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the bread in it} \\
\midrule
el compañero & the one you share it with \\
acompañar & to be that person for somebody \\
el pan & the bread itself \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is the third verb in these chapters built the same way — \textbf{a-} plus a word you own plus \textbf{-ar}, meaning \emph{to make it that}: \emph{acercar} from \emph{cerca}, \emph{acompañar} from \emph{compañero}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
The warmth is not decoration; it decides where the word is used.

At a Spanish funeral the standard thing to say is \textbf{te acompaño en el sentimiento} — \emph{I accompany you in the feeling}. English has no comfortable equivalent and reaches for \emph{I'm sorry for your loss}, which places the speaker outside the grief. The Spanish places them alongside it.

That is worth knowing before you need it, because it is a fixed phrase and improvising in its place is conspicuous.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{acompañar}
  \item will you come with me to the doctor
  \item what the bread is doing inside the word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To go with somebody? (\textbf{Acompañar}.) Which word is inside it? (\emph{\textbf{Compañero}}.) And what is inside that? (\emph{\textbf{Pānis}}, bread.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[directo]{directo — straight through, and live}

\label{lesson:ES-C446-directo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{recto} and \textbf{el tren}. Say \textbf{acompañar}. \emph{Recto} is the shape of a line. Name the word for a train that does not stop.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: directo}
\textbf{directo} — direct, straight through.

\emph{Un tren directo} — a through train, no changes. \emph{Un vuelo directo} — a direct flight. \emph{En directo} — \textbf{live}, on radio or television, which is the use you will meet most.

\emph{Directo} also describes a person: \emph{es muy directo} means blunt, and in Spain it is usually a compliment.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{di-} apart, thoroughly, plus \textbf{-recto}, which you already have.

\emph{Recto} is Latin \textbf{rectus}, straightened, ruled — the participle of \emph{regere}, to rule or guide. To \emph{dirigere} was \textbf{to set something straight}, to aim it, and \emph{directo} is the result of that aiming.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{the straightening in it} \\
\midrule
recto & straight \\
directo & straightened \textbf{towards} \\
dirigir & to direct, to conduct \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English keeps \emph{regere} everywhere once you look: \textbf{correct} (straightened \emph{with}), \textbf{erect} (straightened \emph{up}), \textbf{regular} (by the rule), and \textbf{rule} itself.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{En directo} is the one to fix, because it is not obvious from the parts.

A broadcast \emph{en directo} is going straight from the event to you with nothing in between — no recording, no editing. English calls that \textbf{live}, naming the event; Spanish names the \textbf{path}. Once you see that, \emph{en directo} stops needing translation: the line is straight.

The opposite is \textbf{grabado}, recorded. A Spanish television corner reading \emph{EN DIRECTO} is telling you that what you are watching is happening now.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{directo}
  \item a direct train, no changes
  \item what \emph{en directo} means on a screen
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Direct? (\textbf{Directo}.) Live, on television? (\textbf{En directo}.) Which word you already had is inside it? (\emph{\textbf{Recto}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el partido]{el partido — a side split off}

\label{lesson:ES-C446-partido}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la parte}, \textbf{jugar} and \textbf{el deporte}. Two teams are a whole divided in two. Name what they are about to play.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el partido}
\textbf{el partido} — the match, the game.

\emph{El partido del domingo} — Sunday's match. \emph{¿Viste el partido?} — did you see the match? \emph{Jugar un partido} — to play a game.

It is also \textbf{the political party}: \emph{el partido socialista}. And \emph{sacar partido de algo} is to make the most of something.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{partido} is the past participle of \textbf{partir}, to divide — and \emph{partir} is \textbf{la parte}, which you have.

So \emph{partido} means \textbf{divided}, and everything it names is something a whole was split into.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what it names} & \textbf{what was divided} \\
\midrule
el partido (match) & the players, into two sides \\
el partido (party) & the electorate, into factions \\
sacar partido & the advantage, cut out of a situation \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One word, no coincidence. A football match and a political party are both \emph{a side that a whole was split into}, and English needs two unrelated words — \emph{match}, from an old sense of \emph{equal}, and \emph{party}, which is the same Latin \emph{pars} arriving through French.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Partir} has a second life worth having, because it looks like a contradiction.

\emph{Partir} also means \textbf{to leave, to set off} — \emph{el tren parte a las ocho}. How does \emph{divide} become \emph{depart}?

Because leaving is a division: you separate yourself from the place and the people. English does exactly the same thing and hides it in the Latin — \textbf{depart} is \emph{de-} plus the same \emph{partire}, and \textbf{a parting} is both a splitting and a goodbye.

So a train that \textbf{parte} is cutting itself away from the platform, and a train that is \textbf{directo} does not divide the journey at all. The two words in this chapter that describe a train describe opposite things about it.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el partido}
  \item did you see Sunday's match
  \item why a political party is also \emph{un partido}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The match? (\textbf{El partido}.) What does the word mean literally? (\textbf{Divided}.) What else does \emph{partir} mean? (\textbf{To leave, to set off}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(mirar, mover, acompañar, directo …]{(mirar, mover, acompañar, directo, partido) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R446-repaso-mover}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all five: \emph{to look at}, \emph{to move}, \emph{to go with}, \emph{direct}, \emph{the match}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: you owned four of these already}]
Not one of these five was learned from nothing.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{new word} & \textbf{what you already had} \\
\midrule
\textbf{mirar} & \emph{mira}, the word that opens a sentence \\
\textbf{acompañar} & \emph{el compañero}, and the bread inside it \\
\textbf{directo} & \emph{recto} \\
\textbf{el partido} & \emph{la parte} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Mirar} is the sharpest case. You have been saying \textbf{mira} for chapters as a way of starting a sentence, without being told it is an order from a verb. Finding the verb behind a fixed phrase you already use is one of the cheapest kinds of vocabulary there is, and it has happened three times now — \emph{interesante} gave \emph{interesar}, \emph{el concierto} gave \emph{concertar}, and \emph{mira} gives \emph{mirar}.

When a new word looks like something you say already, check before you learn it twice.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item will you help me move the table
  \item did you see Sunday's match
  \item will you come with me
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You can now arrange to go somewhere with somebody and talk about what you watched.} That is most of what a short message between friends is for.

You also have two distinctions a reader notices. \textbf{Ver} is the eyes receiving and \textbf{mirar} is the eyes aimed. \textbf{Mover} is a thing you could push with your hands and \textbf{trasladar} is an address changing. Both are register rather than grammar, and getting them backwards is the kind of mistake that is understood and still sounds wrong.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Live, on television? (\textbf{En directo}.) To look at, on purpose? (\textbf{Mirar}.) A match, and a political party? (\textbf{Un partido}, for both.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(quedar para el partido) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C446-sintesis-mover}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el partido} and \emph{directo}. Both are in the message below, and one of them is not about a train.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read both, then answer.

\textbf{1 — de Nacho}

\begin{quote}
¿Vemos el \textbf{partido} en mi casa? Lo dan \textbf{en directo} a las nueve. Si quieres \textbf{te acompaño} desde la estación, que el bus de noche no pasa.
\end{quote}

\textbf{2 — la respuesta}

\begin{quote}
Vale. Llego sobre las ocho y media. \textbf{Miro} los horarios y te digo, pero creo que hay un tren \textbf{directo}.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item where they are watching, and at what time
  \item what Nacho offers to do, and why
  \item what the second person is going to check
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Directo} appears twice and means two different things, and nothing but the noun tells you which.

\emph{En directo}, about the match: nothing between the event and the screen — live. \emph{Un tren directo}: nothing between the two stations — no changes. Both are the same picture, a straight line with nothing interrupting it, applied once to time and once to distance. Spanish did not need two words because it named the line rather than the thing.

Then look at \textbf{vemos} and \textbf{miro}. \emph{¿Vemos el partido?} — the match arrives at their eyes, and \emph{ver} is right. \emph{Miro los horarios} — she is aiming her eyes at a timetable on purpose, and \emph{mirar} is right. A Spanish speaker would not swap them, and the pair in one short exchange is the clearest test of the distinction you will get.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Five sentences arranging an evening: say you will watch the match, say it is live, offer to go with somebody, say there is a direct train, and say you will look at the times.

Then check yourself: did you use \textbf{ver} for the match and \textbf{mirar} for the timetable?
\end{tcolorbox}
